steps.working: The white solid is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
steps.decision: Anhydrous means the water has gone. Keep the (II), because copper has more than one oxidation state and the scheme is case- and number-sensitive.

steps.working: hydrated copper(II) sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water
steps.decision: Reactant on the left, both products on the right. The water is a product here, not a spectator, because it has left the crystal.
The question asked for the reversible sign, so it is a mark of its own. Summer 2024's report names the missing equilibrium sign as a common loss.

options: Because the reaction can be driven back by adding water
Because the reaction gives out heat
whyMenu.explain: The sign records that the reverse reaction is real and easy to bring about, not anything about the number of products.

steps.working: Adding water: the white solid turns blue.
steps.decision: Give both colours. 'It turns blue' without saying what it was is worth less than 'white to blue', and a single colour on its own was not accepted in Summer 2024.

steps.working: The tube also becomes hot: heat is given out.
steps.decision: A second observation, and a different kind from the first. Say 'heat given out', not just 'heat', and never 'exothermic', which is a deduction rather than something you can see or feel.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. (b) hydrated copper(II) sulfate ⇌ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate + water. (c) The white solid turns blue and the tube becomes hot, because heat is given out.

A reversible reaction is left to run in a sealed vessel. The graph shows the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction against time.
(a) Describe what happens to each rate during the first minute. [2]
(b) State what is true of the two rates once equilibrium has been reached. [1]
(c) Explain why the amounts of reactants and products then stay constant. [1]

steps.working: The forward rate starts at its highest, 10, and falls.
steps.decision: The forward reaction begins with the most reactant it will ever have, so it starts fastest and slows as the reactants are used up.

steps.working: The reverse rate starts at zero and rises.
steps.decision: At the start there is no product, so there is nothing to react back. As product builds, the reverse reaction speeds up.

steps.working: At 60 s the two rates meet at 4, and from then on they are equal.
steps.decision: Equal rates is the definition. Note that the two curves meet but neither falls to zero: both reactions are still going.

steps.working: Because product is being made as fast as it is being used up, the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.
steps.decision: This is the second half of the definition, and it follows from the first. Summer 2024's report records 'the concentration did not change' being offered in place of the rates, which is this half without the half that explains it.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) The forward rate starts at its highest, 10, and falls; the reverse rate starts at zero and rises. (b) The two rates are equal. (c) Product is formed as fast as it is used up, so the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.

items.stem: In a chemical equation, what does the arrow mean?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — reading an equation; you are not expected to have met equilibrium yet

options.text: turns into
options.feedback: Reactants turn into products. This lesson changes that arrow into one with two heads, and the change of symbol is the whole idea.

options.text: is equal to
options.feedback: An equation balances, but the arrow is not an equals sign: it shows a direction, which is exactly what this topic is about.

options.text: is mixed with
options.feedback: Mixing is what the plus sign shows. The arrow shows the change.

items.stem: What is the rate of a reaction?

options.text: how much change happens in each second
options.feedback: An amount divided by a time. This lesson compares two rates in the same container.

options.text: how much product is made altogether
options.feedback: That is the total, with no time in it. A rate always has a time underneath.

options.text: how long the reaction takes
options.feedback: That is a time on its own. The rate is the change divided by that time.

items.stem: A test tube is sealed with a bung. What can get in or out?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 — open and closed containers

options.text: nothing
options.feedback: Nothing at all. Section 4 calls that a closed system, and equilibrium needs one.

options.text: gases only
options.feedback: A bung stops the gas as well. That is the point of using one, and it is what makes the reverse reaction possible.

options.text: heat only
options.feedback: Heat can still pass through the glass, but no substance can. Closed is about substances.

items.stem: What does a reversible reaction mean?

options.text: the products can react to form the reactants again
options.feedback: Both directions are real, which is why the equation carries a double arrow.

options.text: the reactants can be returned to their original state
options.feedback: 'Original state' is the phrasing Summer 2025 examiners refused. Name the substances: the products react to form the reactants again.

options.text: the reaction can be stopped at any point
options.feedback: Stopping a reaction is not reversing it. Reversible means the products turn back into the reactants.

options.text: the reaction gives out heat one way and takes it in the other
options.feedback: That is true of a reversible reaction, but it is not what the word means. The meaning is about direction, not energy.

items.stem: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated. What is seen, and what is formed?

options.text: blue to white; anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water
options.feedback: Heating drives the water out of the crystals and leaves the white anhydrous solid.

options.text: blue to black; copper(II) oxide and water
options.feedback: Copper(II) oxide is black, but it comes from heating the carbonate. Here the water simply leaves the crystals.

options.text: white to blue; hydrated copper(II) sulfate
options.feedback: That is the reverse change, the one you see when water is added. Heating goes blue to white.

options.text: blue to colourless; copper(II) sulfate solution
options.feedback: A solution is what you get by adding a lot of water. Heating leaves a dry white powder.

items.stem: A reaction in a sealed vessel has reached dynamic equilibrium. Which statement is true?

options.text: the forward and reverse reactions are going at the same rate
options.feedback: Equal rates. Both reactions are still running, which is what the word dynamic records.

options.text: the amounts of reactants and products are equal
options.feedback: The amounts stay constant, but there is no reason for them to be equal to each other. It is the rates that are equal.

options.text: both reactions have stopped
options.feedback: Nothing has stopped. It only looks still because each reaction undoes the other exactly.

options.text: the forward reaction has finished and the reverse one has started
options.feedback: They run at the same time, not one after the other. From the start both are happening.

items.stem: Why must the system be closed for a dynamic equilibrium to be reached?

options.text: so that no substance can escape and the reverse reaction can keep up
options.feedback: A product that has left the container cannot react back, so the two rates could never become equal.

options.text: so that the temperature cannot change
options.feedback: Closed is about substances, not heat. Heat still passes through the glass of a stoppered flask.

options.text: so that the reaction is safe
options.feedback: Safety may be a reason for using a bung, but it is not the reason the definition names.

options.text: so that the forward reaction stops
options.feedback: Neither reaction stops at equilibrium. Closing the system lets the reverse reaction catch up with the forward one.

items.stem: Which set of conditions can be altered to change the direction of a reversible reaction?

options.text: temperature, pressure and concentration
options.feedback: All three. Temperature is the one nearly everybody names; the marks are usually in the other two.

options.text: temperature only
options.feedback: Summer 2025 records exactly this: many named temperature and few mentioned concentration or pressure.

options.text: colour and mass
options.feedback: Colour is something you observe, and mass is conserved. Neither is a condition you set.

options.text: the size of the container only
options.feedback: Changing the container's size changes the pressure, so say pressure — and add temperature and concentration.

items.stem: On the rate-against-time graph for a reversible reaction in a sealed vessel, the two curves meet at 60 s. What is happening at 60 s?
items.skill: Read the equilibrium point from a graph

options.text: the forward and reverse rates have become equal
options.feedback: Both are 4 from then on, and the amounts stop changing.

options.text: the reaction has finished
options.feedback: Neither curve has fallen to zero, so both reactions are still going. They are simply going at the same rate.

options.text: the amounts of reactant and product have become equal
options.feedback: The graph plots rates, not amounts. Equal rates make the amounts constant, not equal.

options.text: the reverse reaction has overtaken the forward one
options.feedback: The curves meet and then run together; neither goes above the other.

parts.stem:
A dynamic equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system.
Explain why.

accepted: no substance can escape, so the products stay in the container and can react back
nothing can get in or out, so the reverse reaction can go on and the two rates can become equal

scheme.for: no substance can enter or escape (the products stay in the container)
so the reverse reaction can take place and the two rates can become equal

hints: Think about what happens to a gas in an open flask.
Which of the two reactions would suffer?
parts.workedSolution: In a closed system no substance can enter or escape, so the products stay in the container and can react back. In an open container the product escapes, the reverse reaction can never catch up, and the two rates never become equal.

pattern.regex: \bkeep the heat in\b|\bkeeps it warm\b|\bso it is safe\b|\bto stop the temperature changing\b

commonErrors.feedback: Closed is about substances, not heat or safety. The reason is that a product which has escaped cannot react back.

parts.stem:
The graph shows the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction for a reversible reaction in a sealed vessel.
Describe how each rate changes, and say what has happened where the two curves meet.

accepted: the forward rate falls, the reverse rate rises from zero, and where they meet the rates are equal so the reaction is at equilibrium
the forward reaction slows down and the reverse reaction speeds up until the two rates are equal, which is dynamic equilibrium

scheme.for: the forward rate starts at its highest and falls (the reactants are being used up)
the reverse rate starts at zero and rises (product is building up)
where the curves meet the two rates are equal, so equilibrium has been reached

hints: Take one curve at a time, then say what their meeting means.
Neither curve reaches zero, so nothing has finished.
parts.workedSolution: The forward rate falls as the reactants are used up, having started at its highest. The reverse rate rises from zero as product builds up. Where the curves meet the two rates are equal, so the reaction has reached dynamic equilibrium and the amounts stop changing.

pattern.regex: \bhas stopped\b|\bhave stopped\b|\bthe reaction ends\b|\bthe reaction finishes\b

commonErrors.feedback: Look at where the curves sit when they meet: both are well above zero, so both reactions are still going. They are simply going at the same rate.

indicativeContent.point: On heating, the blue crystals turn white.
Water is driven off and condenses at the cool end of the tube.
The white solid is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
When water is added the white solid turns blue again.
Heat is given out when the water is added, so the tube becomes hot.
The same reaction has been driven in both directions, so it is reversible.
It is written with the reversible sign rather than a single arrow.

scheme.for: a banded description of both stages and the conclusion: blue to white on heating, water driven off, the white solid named, white to blue on adding water, heat given out, and the deduction that the reaction is reversible and carries the reversible sign
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two stages, and what you would see in each.
Finish with what the two stages together prove.
parts.workedSolution: On heating, the blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate turn white and droplets of water collect at the cool end of the tube, because the water bonded into the crystals is driven off. The white solid left is anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. When water is added to it, the solid turns blue again and the tube becomes hot, because heat is given out. The same reaction has been driven in one direction by heating and in the other by adding water, so it is reversible and is written with the reversible sign rather than a single arrow.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'A reversible reaction in a sealed flask has reached a dynamic equilibrium. Finish this sentence in two ways, giving a statement that is true at that point each time: at equilibrium … [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: … the amounts of the reactants and the products are equal,
… and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The second line is exactly right. The first should be about the rates, not the amounts: at equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions are going at the same rate. The amounts stay constant, but there is no reason at all for them to be equal to each other.
correction: … the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal,
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the two marks. The amounts line stands; the rates line is the one to fix. Summer 2024 examiners saw the same swap again and again, with the concentration written where the rates belonged. Rates first, amounts second, every time.

prompts.answer: One that can go in both directions: the reactants form the products, and the products can react to form the reactants again.

prompts.prompt: What sign is used in place of the usual arrow in a reversible reaction, and why is it worth a mark?
prompts.answer: The reversible sign, a double arrow. It records that both reactions happen, so a single arrow is a different claim and earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated. What is seen, what is formed, and what happens if water is added afterwards?
prompts.answer: Blue turns white and water is driven off, leaving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Adding water turns it blue again and gives out heat.
In a closed system, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal and the amounts of reactants and products remain constant.

prompts.prompt: At equilibrium, what is equal and what is constant?
prompts.answer: The rates of the two reactions are equal; the amounts of reactants and products are constant. The amounts are not equal to each other.

prompts.prompt: Name the three conditions that can be altered to change the direction of a reversible reaction.
Why must a system be closed before it can reach a dynamic equilibrium?
prompts.answer: Nothing can enter or escape, so the products stay in the container and can react back. In an open container the product escapes and the reverse reaction never catches up.

prompts.prompt: Why is the equilibrium called dynamic rather than still?
prompts.answer: Both reactions are still going at equilibrium, at the same rate as each other, so nothing has stopped even though nothing appears to change.
